title: The blackout-box mystery
subtitle: Spring 1 • Week 6 • Explain the missing view
objective: Explain why an object needs light reaching it and then the eye to be seen.

sow.exactOutcome: Recognise that we need light to see and that dark is the absence of light.
sow.alignment: Direct match to the named outcome. The lesson is a 40-minute exemplar, with optional greater depth; no accreditation completion is claimed.

priorLearning: Everyday objects can be described by what we observe.
Use a labelled diagram or evidence card to explain a choice.
success: Identify that light is needed to see.
Explain that light enters the eye.
Distinguish dim light from complete darkness.

vocabulary.meaning: Something that gives out its own light.
To send light back from a surface.
An absence of light; a dim place still has some light.

equipment: Low-power battery LED torch; white card; familiar small object; optional pre-made viewing box; printed evidence.
preparation: Prepare a box with separate viewing and light openings, both adult-cut. Keep the room comfortably lit.
Test visibility before the lesson. The box may leak light: treat this as a limitation, not pupil error.
safety: No dark-room requirement or blindfolds. Keep exits and walkways lit.
Use a cool, low-power LED; never aim it into eyes. No lasers, hot lamps or direct Sun viewing.
Adult prepares any holes. Offer the paper route to anyone uncomfortable with a viewing box.
practicalAlternative: Use the four constructed box cases; all tasks can be completed without looking into a box.

misconceptions.claim: Eyes send out light to find objects.
misconceptions.correction: Light enters the eye from a source or a reflecting object.
misconceptions.check: Ask which way the arrow points at the eye.

misconceptions.claim: Waiting lets you see when there is no light at all.
misconceptions.correction: Eyes adapt to dim light; they cannot see an object in complete darkness.
misconceptions.check: Compare a dim room with the ideal no-light case.

access.supported: Choose one route: short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed explanation; keep the same science goal.
access.standard: Use the evidence provided to record a decision and explain the science in short sentences.
access.stretch: Apply the same core idea to a changed setup, identify a limitation and justify a better decision.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence and equipment. Offer seated observation, a quiet paper route, partner rehearsal and a pass. Never require public performance or a darkened room.

sources.title: Department for Education: science programmes of study
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Year 3 light outcomes anchor the BUILD content; ray explanations are carefully modelled as an accessible extension.

slides.title: An object is inside. Why can’t we see it?
slides.notes: Show the optional box or describe its two openings. Do not reveal the object by touch. State the objective and offer paper-only observation.

slides.title: What do we already know?
body: 1. Name something that gives out light.
2. Can a plain card make its own light?
slides.notes: Accept lit lamp, Sun or other valid source. Plain card reflects rather than produces visible light. Eyes enable sight; other senses can identify an object without seeing it.

slides.title: I follow the light
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I start at the source, not the eye. I trace light to the object, then into the eye. Now the object can be seen.” Arrows are selected light paths, not all light. Never demonstrate by shining into anyone’s eye.

visual.title: Light reaches your eye
visual.description: A ray travels from the LED source to an object; reflected light then enters an eye. The eye does not send light out.

elements.text:
Some reflected light
enters the eye.
The eye receives light. Arrows show its direction.

slides.title: I remove the source
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I keep the object in place. In this ideal model, no light comes from anywhere. I remove the light arrows. I cannot infer the object has gone merely because it cannot be seen.” A real box can leak dim light.

visual.title: No light: no visual information
visual.description: An unlit LED, an object and an eye have no light-path arrows. This ideal model excludes all other light.

elements.text: No light reaches the object or the eye.

slides.title: I block one part of the path
body: A card can stop this light.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “The card blocks our source. If room light entered elsewhere, we might still see the object. My model therefore says no other light.”

visual.title: A path can be blocked
visual.description: An opaque card stops the source-to-object path. No other light source is included in this model.

elements.text:
In this model, no other
light lights the object.
Removing the block can restore the light path.

slides.title: The case conference
slides.notes: Partners take predictor and evidence-reader roles. A and B use the same white object. The source changes; the object remains. Invite an individual choice before the shared answer.

rows: All light openings sealed; torch off
Torch lights object; viewing opening clear
table.caption: Constructed teaching evidence

slides.prompt: W1. Which change explains the new view?
slides.reveal: B adds a light path from source to object to eye.

slides.title: Repair the explanation
body: C: a small light leak; object faintly seen.
D: no light at all; wait one minute.
slides.notes: Read cards C and D from the shared page. Ask pairs to replace “eyes make more light” with an accurate explanation. A faint view means some light reaches the eye. Complete darkness stays without visible detail.
slides.prompt: W2. Why are C and D different?
slides.reveal: C has a little light. D has none; waiting alone does not add light.

slides.title: What makes seeing possible?
slides.notes: If pupils choose eyes sending light, trace the final arrow into the eye together. If they choose waiting, compare dim and no-light cases.

options.text: Our eyes send light onto the object.
options.feedback: For seeing, light enters our eyes; they do not illuminate the object.

options.text: Light from the object enters our eyes.
options.feedback: The object can give out light or reflect light from a source.

options.text: Waiting makes light appear in total darkness.
options.feedback: Adaptation helps with dim light, but it cannot create light.

slides.title: Choose your investigation route
slides.notes: Give one route only, selected with the pupil. The shared evidence page supports every route. Optional observation: compare a covered light opening with the LED lighting the object. Never claim a practical box is perfectly dark without evidence. Pupils can use only the cases.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Read or point to one clue.
slides.notes: Shares the 12-minute independent stage. Optional observation: compare a covered light opening with the LED lighting the object. Never claim a practical box is perfectly dark without evidence. Pupils can use only the cases.

slides.title: Make your own science record
body: Use a diagram, words or speech.
Check one answer with the evidence.
slides.notes: Allow ten minutes of independent response after the two-minute setup. Optional observation: compare a covered light opening with the LED lighting the object. Never claim a practical box is perfectly dark without evidence. Pupils can use only the cases.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: Does my answer match the evidence?
slides.notes: Shares the independent stage. Ask the pupil to point to the clue supporting their answer; accept a spoken correction or changed choice.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve our account
body: Choose how to share one idea.
Use evidence to improve our account.
slides.notes: Give a private or paired option. Adopt one scientifically sound pupil revision in the class explanation and name the change. No public ranking.
slides.reveal: Light reaches the object, and some reflected light enters the eye.

slides.title: Three quick checks
body: E1. What do we need in order to see?
E2. Does light enter or leave the eye when we see?
E3. Can we see an object with no light at all?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual answers. Secure core requires the main idea and a relevant reason. Revisit the relevant worked diagram next lesson if the explanation reverses cause and effect.
slides.reveal: See the teacher answer guide for the three checks.

pupilPages.title: Evidence: four box cases
pupilPages.intro: Constructed teaching cases. The same non-glowing white object stays inside.

cards.title: A • Light sealed out
cards.text: Torch off. No light enters. Object is not visible.

cards.title: B • Torch lights the object
cards.text: Torch on, aimed at the object. The viewing path is clear. Object is visible.

cards.title: C • A small light leak
cards.text: Torch off, but some room light enters. The object is faintly visible.

cards.title: D • Wait in no light
cards.text: No light enters. After one minute the object still cannot be seen.

blocks.prompt: W1. Compare A and B. What changed?
W2. Explain why C is different from D.

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Find the light
pupilPages.intro: Use cards A–D. Word bank: light / object / eye / darkness.

blocks.prompt: S1. In which case is the object clearly visible?
S2. Complete: We need __ to see.
S3. Add arrows to show the order: source → object → __.
S4. A place has a little light. Is it dim or completely dark?
S5. Explain why waiting does not make D visible.

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Explain the evidence
pupilPages.intro: Make a short record from the case cards.

blocks.prompt: T2. Draw and label a light path that lets us see the object.
T3. A pupil says the object disappears in A. Correct the claim.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Diagnose a leaky box
pupilPages.intro: A team says its box has no light. They can still faintly see a white object.

blocks.prompt: X1. Explain why their observation challenges their no-light claim.
X2. Suggest one possible route by which light enters.
X3. Predict what happens if that route is fully blocked and no other light enters.
X4. Explain why identifying the object by touch is not evidence that it can be seen.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. What do we need in order to see?
E2. Does light enter or leave the eye when we see?
E3. Can we see an object with no light at all?
R1. Which idea did you improve after hearing evidence?
R2. What would you investigate or ask next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 Lit lamp, Sun or another valid source. 2 No, ordinary card reflects light. 3 Sight.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 The torch provides light; the object stays. W2 C has a small light leak; D excludes all light. Seeing C does not show that eyes generate light.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: The second option is correct. Light enters eyes. Waiting helps adaptation only when some light is present.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 B. S2 light. S3 eye. S4 dim. S5 No light has been added; eyes cannot see the object without light.

answers.label: T1–T3
answers.answer: T1 A: no light path; B: torch to object to eye; C: some room light enters and reflects; D: no light, even after waiting. T2 arrows source→object→eye. T3 the object remains present but is not visible.

answers.label: X1–X4
answers.answer: X1 Seeing the non-glowing object means some light reaches the eye. X2 a gap at the lid, light opening or viewing opening. X3 no visible view of the object. X4 touch uses a different sense, so it can support the object’s presence without showing a light path.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 light. E2 enters. E3 no. Accept a diagram or spoken explanation.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a science-related revision or relevant next question. A pass or private response is acceptable; preferences have no fixed right answer.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 7; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 12; review 3; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the stage time.
BUILD follows the user’s Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful materials for secondary pupils. Routes are adjustable access choices, not fixed groups or diagnoses.
Every core task can run from the printed evidence. Do not present constructed teaching evidence as observations pupils made. A pupil’s spoken reasoning carries the same scientific value as writing.
Secure core: light is needed and enters the eye. The distinction between dim and complete darkness is an explanatory extension; do not require advanced eye adaptation terminology.

HTML We do: pupils choose a prediction, test it against the user-controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. The shared paper cases and W1/W2 prompts provide the equivalent classroom discussion without a device. Any animation is a teaching model, not filmed experimental evidence.

interactive.title: Repair the missing light path
interactive.intro: Predict each case, then test the model. These are constructed cases, not a live camera view.

steps.question: Case A: all light is excluded. What will be visible?

choices.text: No view of the non-glowing object
choices.feedback: No light from the object reaches the eye.
Waiting cannot create light in complete darkness.

visual.title: No light: no visual information
visual.description: An unlit LED, an object and an eye have no light-path arrows. This ideal model excludes all other light.

elements.text: No light reaches the object or the eye.

steps.explanation: Case A: the object remains present, but no light reaches the eye.

steps.question: Case B: the LED lights the object and the viewing path is clear. What changes?

choices.feedback: Some light reflects from the object into the eye.
The eyes receive the reflected light; they do not illuminate the object.

visual.title: Light reaches your eye
visual.description: A ray travels from the LED source to an object; reflected light then enters an eye. The eye does not send light out.

elements.text:
Some reflected light
enters the eye.
The eye receives light. Arrows show its direction.

steps.explanation: Case B: source → object → eye. This is the light path explaining the view.

steps.question: An opaque card blocks the only source-to-object path. What will restore the view?

choices.feedback: This restores the path so light can reach the object and eye.

choices.text: Wait with the path still blocked
choices.feedback: Waiting does not add another light path.

visual.title: A path can be blocked
visual.description: An opaque card stops the source-to-object path. No other light source is included in this model.

elements.text:
In this model, no other
light lights the object.
Removing the block can restore the light path.

steps.explanation: With no other source, removing the block restores the path. Case C in the paper evidence differs because some room light enters.
